title: Challenges to Indian Democracy
summary: Abraham Lincoln: 'Democracy is a government of the people, by the people and for the people.' The word comes from the Greek 'demokratia' — 'demos' (people) and 'kratos' (power). Democracy is a form of government in which supreme power rests with the people, exercised directly or through elected representatives in periodic free elections. But it is more than a form of government: it is also a type of state, a social system, an economic order and a way of life reflecting equality, liberty, fraternity, secularism and justice in society and in individual behaviour.

Essential conditions: political — a Constitution vesting power in the people and protecting rights; universal adult franchise; participation of all citizens; a responsible government (executive answerable to the legislature, legislature to the people) and an independent judiciary; working parties and pressure groups; free press and enlightened public opinion (political democracy). Social and economic — equality of status and opportunity, social security and welfare, universal education and the fruits of development reaching the poor (social democracy).

India has held free and fair elections from panchayats to the President, seen peaceful transfers of power (unlike military coups in some neighbours), effective legislatures, an independent judiciary and a free media; laws like the RTI Act 2005 and RTE Act 2009 have empowered people.

1. Illiteracy: literacy was only 18.33% in 1951 (women 8.9%). Voters showed maturity anyway (e.g. rejecting the Congress in 1977 after the Emergency), but literacy is needed to understand issues and rights. In 2011 literacy was 74.04% (female 65.46%, male 82.14%).

2. Poverty: 'for a hungry person the right to vote has no meaning' — poverty is the greatest bane of democracy and the root of other deprivations. The poverty line was based on calories: 2,400 per day in rural and 2,100 in urban areas; later clothing, shelter and education were added. Poverty was estimated at 27.5% in 2004–05; India ranked 134 of 182 on the Human Development Index (2009). Causes: unemployment and under-employment, population growth and unequal development.

3. Gender discrimination: shown by the sex ratio (972 in 1901, 940 in 2011; Haryana 877), the child sex ratio (914 in 2011, down from 927), female foeticide, high infant and maternal mortality, lower female literacy and low representation of women. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1993) reserved one-third of seats for women in panchayats and municipalities; some States (Bihar etc.) give 50%. The Women's Reservation Bill for Parliament was pending when the textbook was written (it was passed in 2023).

4. Casteism, communalism and religious fundamentalism: untouchability persists despite the ban; the 'politicisation of caste' and 'casteisation of politics' and caste vote-banks keep inequalities alive and hinder democratic ideals. Communalism — political loyalty to one religious community against others — causes riots and is opposed to secularism; fundamentalism demands strict orthodoxy and opposes reform.

5. Regionalism: regional disparities in income, literacy, health and industry cause feelings of neglect, leading to demands for new States, autonomy or even secession (militancy in J&K, ULFA in Assam). Defending regional interests is natural, but becomes harmful when politicised.

6. Corruption: India ranked 95 of 183 on Transparency International's index (2011); a nexus of politicians, bureaucrats and industrialists; bribing of voters. 7. Criminalisation of politics: criminals contesting and influencing elections; courts and voters must check it. 8. Political violence: communal and caste violence, violence in elections, in demands for new States, strikes and agitations.

Universal literacy: free and compulsory education to 14 years; the National Literacy Mission (1988) after the National Policy on Education 1986; Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan for 6–14-year-olds; Saakshar Bharat for adults over 15; the RTE Act 2009.

Poverty alleviation: programmes giving assets and skills (Swarnajayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana with self-help groups) and wage employment (Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana, Employment Assurance Scheme, MGNREGA guaranteeing 100 days of work a year to a rural household).

Removing gender discrimination: the 73rd and 74th Amendments; the National Policy for the Empowerment of Women (2001) — equal access to decision-making, health, education, jobs and equal pay, stronger laws, and ending violence against women and girls.

Removing regional imbalances: Tribal, Hill Area, Border Area, Western Ghats, Drought Prone Area and Desert Development Programmes and special funds for the North-East; good local leadership. Administrative reforms (accountable, transparent, citizen-friendly, decentralised administration and e-governance) and judicial reforms (simpler procedures, more judges, filling vacancies, transparency and accountability). Sustainable development — meeting present needs without compromising future generations (Brundtland Commission, 1987).

Citizens must participate — vote wisely and join parties and civil society organisations; make the system accountable using the RTI Act, the media, peaceful protest and satyagraha; and fulfil obligations — freedom is not absolute and must not infringe others' rights. They should respect the law, reject violence, respect others' dignity and views, negotiate and cooperate, and assert their opinion.

vsa: What do you mean by political democracy and social democracy?

Political democracy has political conditions — a Constitution vesting power in the people, fundamental rights, universal adult franchise, a responsible government and free press. Social democracy means equality of social status and opportunity, social welfare and economic development reaching everyone, especially the poor.
Explain any two essential conditions for democracy.

(1) A Constitution that vests supreme power in the people and protects rights, with universal adult franchise and regular free elections. (2) Social and economic equality — education for all, social security and the fruits of development reaching the poor; also a responsible government and a free press.
What is meant by criminalisation of politics? How can it be checked?

Criminalisation of politics means people with criminal records contesting and influencing elections and entering legislatures, which negates democratic values. It can be checked by the courts and the Election Commission (disqualifying such candidates) and above all by voters refusing to elect them.
Why is poverty called the greatest bane of democracy?

A hungry person cares first for food, so the right to vote means little to him. Poverty denies people opportunities for a healthy, fulfilling life, keeps them unequal and dependent, and they can be bribed or exploited during elections.
sa: Suggest any three ways to strengthen Indian democracy.

(1) Achieve universal literacy and reduce poverty and inequality so that every citizen can participate meaningfully. (2) Check corruption, criminalisation of politics and the use of caste and religion in elections through electoral, administrative and judicial reforms. (3) Citizens must vote wisely, use the RTI Act and peaceful protest to keep representatives accountable, and respect others' rights and views.
October 2025

or: Suggest any three ways to empower women.

(1) Education and skills for girls, with equal access to health care and jobs and equal pay. (2) Political empowerment through reservation in panchayats, municipalities and legislatures. (3) Strict enforcement of laws against foeticide, dowry and violence, and changing attitudes so that girls and boys are treated equally (National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001).

sa: How is casteism a challenge to Indian democracy? Explain in three points.

(1) Untouchability and caste discrimination persist despite the constitutional ban, denying Dalits dignity and opportunities. (2) Politicisation of caste and 'casteisation of politics' — parties use caste as vote-banks for narrow gains, weakening issues-based politics. (3) It keeps socio-economic inequalities alive and sometimes causes caste violence, against the democratic ideals of equality and fraternity.
April 2025

or: How is criminalisation of politics a challenge to Indian democracy? Explain in three points.

(1) People with criminal records contest and win elections using money and muscle power, negating democratic values. (2) Violence and intimidation stop voters from voting freely and spoil free and fair elections. (3) Criminals in power protect lawbreakers, increase corruption and reduce public trust; courts and alert voters must reject such candidates.

sa: Suggest any three corrective measures for universal literacy (education for all).

(1) Free and compulsory education for all children of 6–14 years under the RTE Act 2009 and Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan. (2) Adult literacy through the National Literacy Mission and Saakshar Bharat (functional literacy for those above 15). (3) Special attention to girls and disadvantaged groups — scholarships, mid-day meals, more schools in remote areas.
April 2025
October 2017
Explain any three tools available to a common citizen for making the government accountable.

(1) The vote — citizens can remove a government that does not perform. (2) The Right to Information Act 2005 — to ask for information on government decisions and spending. (3) The media, petitions, civil society organisations and peaceful protest, satyagraha or civil disobedience to point out failures and demand action.
October 2024
'Discrimination against girls and women exists in every walk of life.' Support the statement.

(1) The declining sex ratio (940 in 2011) and child sex ratio (914) show son preference, female foeticide and neglect of girls. (2) Female literacy (65.46%) is far below male literacy (82.14%), and girls do more household work while boys go to school. (3) Women get fewer jobs, lower pay and little representation in Parliament and public life; maternal mortality is high.
April 2021
October 2016
How does literacy play an important role in the success of a democracy?

(1) Literate citizens understand issues, policies and candidates and vote wisely. (2) They know their rights and duties and principles of liberty and equality, so they can make representatives accountable. (3) They take part in public life, resist exploitation and support development; that is why universal literacy is a must for democracy.
October 2021
la: What are the major challenges faced by Indian democracy? Explain any six.

(1) Illiteracy — many cannot fully understand issues and rights. (2) Poverty and unemployment — the greatest bane of democracy. (3) Gender discrimination — low sex ratio, female literacy and representation. (4) Casteism, communalism and religious fundamentalism — vote-banks, riots and inequality. (5) Regionalism arising from regional imbalances, sometimes leading to separatism. (6) Corruption, criminalisation of politics and political violence, which undermine free elections and trust in institutions.
What corrective measures are needed to meet the challenges to Indian democracy?

(1) Universal literacy — RTE Act, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, Saakshar Bharat. (2) Poverty alleviation — self-employment (SGSY, self-help groups) and wage employment (MGNREGA). (3) Elimination of gender discrimination — 73rd/74th Amendments, National Policy for Empowerment of Women 2001. (4) Removal of regional imbalance — Tribal, Hill, Border, Desert and Drought-Prone Area programmes. (5) Administrative and judicial reforms — accountable, transparent, e-governance; faster justice and more judges. (6) Sustainable development and an active role of citizens in participation and accountability.
